I am 66 years old, and I have never been to school. I cannot read, but I know my land. I have farmed these fields for 45 years, and my mother and father did the same before me. My farm is just under 12 mu, and I plant wheat in autumn and maize in summer — that is what everyone around here does, and I do not try to be clever.

For my wheat, I will plant the same improved variety that my neighbor Li uses. Last year I got about 500 jin per mu, and this year I want the same or a little better. I sow about 30 jin of seed per mu. At sowing time, I put one full bag of compound fertilizer on each mu — that is 50 jin per mu. I do not know what the numbers on the bag mean, but the dealer gives me the red bags, and I have used them for years. When the wheat turns green in March, I spread half a bag of urea on each mu, and at jointing I spread another half bag. That is one bag of compound and one bag of urea total for each mu of wheat. I would rather put a little too much than watch my wheat turn yellow and lose the harvest. My well water is good, so I irrigate three times: once before winter to help the wheat survive, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I spray three times — herbicide once when the weeds come up, and insecticide twice because the aphids get bad some years. Before I sow the wheat, I plough the field deep to bury the maize stubble.

For the maize, as soon as the wheat is cut in June, I hire the rotary tiller to go over the field. I plant hybrid maize seed — about 4 jin per mu. I put one bag of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, just like for the wheat. Then when the maize is knee-high, I cultivate between the rows and side-dress half a bag of urea per mu. Some years I add another half bag if the leaves look pale, but I will decide when I see it. Maize does not need as much water as wheat, so I irrigate twice — once when it is shooting up, and once when the tassels are out. I spray twice for pests. Last year my maize gave me about 600 jin per mu, and if the weather holds I expect the same this year.

My son wanted me to cut back on fertilizer to save money, but I told him: a bad harvest means we lose everything. Wasting a few jin of fertilizer is nothing compared to an empty grain sack.
